questions.stem: Which offence is best classified as an offence against the sovereign?
options: Assault occasioning bodily harm
Possession of a prohibited drug
Treason against the Commonwealth
Fraud against a private business owner
questions.explanation: Offences against the sovereign threaten the state or its system of government, with treason and sedition the classic examples. Fraud against a company is an economic offence, and assault is an offence against the person.

questions.stem: A company director secretly moves investors' money into her own accounts over several years. Which category of crime does this best illustrate?
options: A preliminary offence
White-collar crime
A public order offence
A crime against the person
questions.explanation: White-collar crime is non-violent crime committed by people in positions of trust or business, such as fraud, embezzlement and insider trading. A preliminary offence is an incomplete crime such as an attempt or conspiracy, which does not fit a completed fraud.

questions.stem: Which crime is an example of a preliminary (inchoate) offence?
options: Damaging a bus shelter with graffiti
Driving with a prescribed blood alcohol
Conspiring with others to import drugs
Stealing a car from a shopping centre
questions.explanation: Preliminary offences, such as attempt and conspiracy, are committed even though the planned crime is not completed, so police can step in early. Stealing a car and damaging property are completed offences against property.

questions.stem: Which development best illustrates the changing nature of crime affecting individuals and society?
options: The use of the Local Court to hear most summary offences in NSW
Scams and identity theft carried out online by offenders in other countries
A long-term fall in the number of people convicted of theft in shops
The continued use of juries in trials for the most serious offences
questions.explanation: Technology has created new ways to commit old crimes such as fraud, and offenders overseas are hard to investigate and prosecute, so the law has had to adapt. Juries and the Local Court are features of court procedure, not changes in the nature of crime.

questions.stem: Research shows higher offending rates among young people who left school early and are unemployed. Which factor affecting criminal behaviour does this best illustrate?
options: Social and economic factors
Genetic factors
Political factors
Self-interest alone
questions.explanation: Disadvantage such as low education, unemployment and poverty is a social and economic factor linked to higher offending. Genetic factors concern inherited traits, and political factors involve offending to achieve a political goal.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains why criminologists are cautious about genetic explanations of criminal behaviour?
options: Genetic testing has proved that no inherited trait has any link to human behaviour, so the theory has been abandoned
Courts in NSW are required by statute to reduce every sentence where an offender has a genetic predisposition
Genetic factors only explain white-collar crime, so they cannot be used to explain crimes against the person
Any inherited tendency interacts with upbringing and environment, so genes alone cannot explain why a person offends
questions.explanation: Most research treats criminal behaviour as the product of many interacting factors, so an inherited tendency is at most one influence among social, economic and psychological ones. No statute requires a reduction for genetic predisposition, and research has not ruled out every link.

questions.stem: Which measure is an example of situational crime prevention?
options: Offering drug rehabilitation to people with addictions
Installing CCTV and better lighting in a train station car park
Funding after-school programs for young people at risk
Running parenting courses in disadvantaged communities
questions.explanation: Situational crime prevention changes the immediate environment to reduce the opportunity to offend and increase the risk of being caught. Youth programs, parenting courses and rehabilitation tackle underlying causes, which is social crime prevention.

questions.stem: A council funds a youth centre, job training and a mentoring program in a suburb with high youth crime. Which form of crime prevention is this?
options: Situational crime prevention
General deterrence
Police discretion
Social crime prevention
questions.explanation: Social crime prevention addresses the social and economic causes of crime, such as disadvantage and lack of opportunity. Situational prevention would change the physical setting, for example with locks or cameras.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates situational crime prevention?
options: It removes the underlying causes of offending, but it takes decades before any effect on crime rates can be measured
It is the only form of crime prevention allowed under NSW law, so its effectiveness is not open to debate in practice
It relies on courts to impose longer prison sentences, so it has no role for local councils, businesses or individual citizens
It can quickly reduce crime in a targeted place, but offending may move to other areas without its causes being addressed
questions.explanation: Cameras, locks and lighting can make a place harder to target almost at once, but critics point to displacement, where offenders simply move elsewhere. Addressing causes over the long term is the strength of social crime prevention, not situational prevention.

questions.stem: In NSW, the main Act setting out police powers to arrest, search and detain people is the:
options: Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002
Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999
Criminal Procedure Act 1986
Bail Act 2013
questions.explanation: The Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002, known as LEPRA, brings most NSW police powers and safeguards into one Act. The Criminal Procedure Act deals with how proceedings run in court, and the Bail Act deals with release before trial.

questions.stem: Why is it important to the rule of law that police powers are set out in legislation and limited by safeguards?
options: Police can then use any method they choose so long as the person they arrest is later found guilty
Courts no longer need to consider whether evidence was obtained lawfully once police powers are written down
Members of the public are then required to answer every police question about any offence they witnessed
Police act only within the powers the law gives them and can be held accountable if they exceed them
questions.explanation: The rule of law requires that everyone, including the state and its officers, is subject to the law. Clear statutory limits let courts exclude improperly obtained evidence and let people complain about misuse of power.

questions.stem: Under section 99 of LEPRA, a police officer may arrest a person without a warrant if the officer suspects on reasonable grounds that the person committed an offence and:
options: has obtained written approval from the Director of Public Prosecutions before taking the person into custody
knows the person has refused to give their name and address, which is the only reason allowed by the Act
is satisfied the arrest is reasonably necessary for a reason set out in the Act, such as to stop the offence continuing
believes the person has previously been convicted of any offence, even if it is quite unrelated to the current suspicion
questions.explanation: Section 99 requires both a reasonable suspicion and that the arrest is reasonably necessary for a listed purpose, such as stopping the offence, preventing flight, ensuring court attendance or protecting evidence or safety. Arrest is meant to be a last resort, not routine, and refusing to give a name is only one listed reason.

questions.stem: Who issues a search warrant to NSW police?
options: The Director of Public Prosecutions
The Attorney General of New South Wales in person
An authorised officer such as a magistrate
The Commissioner of Police in writing
questions.explanation: A search warrant is granted by an independent authorised officer, such as a magistrate or authorised registrar, who must be satisfied there are reasonable grounds. This independent check protects privacy against the police acting on their own say-so.

questions.stem: A police officer stops a man in the street and searches his bag without a warrant. Under LEPRA, the search is lawful only if the officer:
options: intends to issue him with a penalty notice for an unrelated traffic offence once the search has been completed
suspects on reasonable grounds that he has something such as a prohibited drug, a stolen item or a dangerous article
has a personal feeling that he looks out of place in the area, even without any facts to support the feeling
has first obtained the written permission of a magistrate by telephone, which the Act requires for every personal search
questions.explanation: LEPRA allows a personal search without warrant when an officer suspects on reasonable grounds that the person has items such as stolen property, prohibited drugs or dangerous implements. A hunch without facts is not reasonable suspicion, and a warrant is not needed for a lawful personal search.

questions.stem: Under Part 9 of LEPRA, how long may police detain an arrested person to investigate an offence before a detention warrant is needed?
options: A reasonable time of up to 24 hours, not counting certain time-outs
Up to four days, provided the person is told the reason for detention
As long as is needed, provided a lawyer is present throughout
A reasonable time of up to six hours, not counting certain time-outs
questions.explanation: The investigation period is a reasonable time of up to six hours, and periods such as travel to the station, medical treatment or speaking to a lawyer are excluded. Police may apply to an authorised officer for a detention warrant to extend the period.

questions.stem: Police want to keep questioning a suspect beyond the investigation period allowed under Part 9 of LEPRA. What must they do?
options: Obtain the suspect's written consent, which allows detention to continue until the questioning has ended
Notify the Director of Public Prosecutions, who may extend detention for as long as the case requires
Apply to an authorised officer for a detention warrant, which can extend the period once by up to six hours
Charge the suspect with a minor offence, which automatically restarts the whole investigation period from zero
questions.explanation: A detention warrant can be granted only once and adds up to six hours, so the usual maximum is 12 hours of investigation time. Neither consent nor a holding charge lets police avoid these limits, which protect liberty and guard against oppressive questioning.

questions.stem: When a person is detained at a NSW police station after arrest, the custody manager must:
options: keep the arrest secret from the person's family until the full investigation period has ended
caution the person and give them a summary of their rights, such as the right to contact a friend or lawyer
conduct the questioning personally so that the investigating officers cannot influence what the person says
decide whether the person is guilty before deciding whether to refuse or grant the person police bail
questions.explanation: The custody manager is an officer independent of the investigation who looks after the detained person's welfare and rights, including giving a caution and a summary of Part 9. The detained person may communicate with a friend, relative, guardian or lawyer, and guilt is a matter for the courts.

questions.stem: Before exercising a power such as a search or a direction to move on, a NSW police officer must generally:
options: give their name and place of duty and the reason for using the power
show the person a warrant signed by a magistrate for that particular power
ask a second officer to confirm that the power may be used
warn the person that they will be charged if they ask questions
questions.explanation: LEPRA requires officers to provide their name, place of duty and the reason for exercising many powers, and to show identification if not in uniform. This safeguard makes police accountable, while many powers can be used without a warrant.

questions.stem: Police discretion is best described as:
options: the power of police to refuse to give evidence in court about how they conducted an investigation
the power of police to decide how to deal with an incident, such as whether to warn, caution, fine or charge
the power of police to decide the sentence an offender receives once the offender has pleaded guilty in court
the duty of police to arrest every person they suspect of an offence, however minor the offence may be
questions.explanation: Officers regularly choose between options such as taking no action, giving a warning or caution, issuing a penalty notice, or charging. Sentencing is for the courts, and police are not required to arrest for every suspected offence.

questions.stem: An officer finds an adult using offensive language in public and issues an on-the-spot fine instead of charging him. What does this best show about police discretion?
options: It shows that police cannot deal with any offence unless a magistrate has first approved how it is handled
It saves court time and resources for minor offences, but it relies on officers using their judgment consistently
It means the man now has a conviction recorded against him for the offence, just as if he had gone to court
It takes away the man's right to dispute the matter, because a penalty notice can never be challenged in any court
questions.explanation: Penalty notices and criminal infringement notices deal with minor offences quickly without a court hearing, but discretion can be applied unevenly, which raises concerns about equality before the law. Paying a penalty notice does not result in a conviction, and a person can elect to have the matter heard in court.

questions.stem: Which concern about police discretion is most strongly supported by evidence that some groups are searched and charged at higher rates than others for similar conduct?
options: Discretion removes the presumption of innocence for every person who is arrested
Discretion lets police impose prison sentences without the involvement of a court
Discretion prevents victims from reporting offences to the police in the first place
Discretion can be used inconsistently, which undermines equality before the law
questions.explanation: When similar conduct is treated differently depending on who the person is, the principle that everyone is equal before the law is weakened. Discretion does not give police sentencing power or remove the presumption of innocence.

questions.stem: The right to silence means that a person suspected of an offence:
options: may refuse to give their name to police in all circumstances, whatever the offence
generally does not have to answer police questions or give evidence at their own trial
must answer every question police ask, but may stay silent once the trial has started
cannot be asked any questions by police until a magistrate has authorised the interview
questions.explanation: The right to silence protects people from being forced to incriminate themselves, which supports the presumption of innocence. Some laws do require a person to give their name and address in certain situations, so that right is not unlimited.

questions.stem: Under section 89A of the Evidence Act 1995 (NSW), a court may allow an unfavourable inference to be drawn from an adult suspect's silence only if, among other conditions:
options: a special caution was given for a serious indictable offence while a lawyer was present, and the accused later relies on a fact not mentioned
the accused refused to give their name to police at the time of arrest, whatever the offence and whether or not a lawyer was present
the police officer believed the accused was guilty and recorded that belief in writing before the interview began
the accused was charged with a summary offence and had been given an ordinary caution at the start of the interview
questions.explanation: Section 89A, added in 2013, is a limited exception to the right to silence: it applies only to serious indictable offences, adult suspects, a special caution and a lawyer being present, where the accused later relies on a fact they could reasonably have mentioned. In other cases, section 89 says no unfavourable inference may be drawn from silence.

questions.stem: Which right of an accused person most directly supports the presumption of innocence during police questioning?
options: The right to a jury of twelve
The right to appeal a sentence
The right to a public hearing
The right to silence
questions.explanation: Because the prosecution must prove guilt, the accused cannot be forced to help build the case against them, which the right to silence protects. A jury, an appeal and a public hearing protect fairness at later stages rather than during questioning.

questions.stem: When an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander person is taken into custody in NSW, police must notify the Aboriginal Legal Service. What is the main purpose of this?
options: So the person can quickly get legal advice and a welfare check while in custody
So the person can be released at once without any charge being laid against them
So the Aboriginal Legal Service can decide whether the person should be charged
So the person's case will be heard by a jury made up only of community members
questions.explanation: The Custody Notification Service gives detained Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people prompt legal advice and a welfare check, a measure linked to the Royal Commission into Aboriginal Deaths in Custody. It does not decide charges or change who sits on a jury.

questions.stem: In NSW, the Charter of Victims Rights is set out in the:
options: Bail Act 2013
Victims Rights and Support Act 2013
Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999
Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002
questions.explanation: The Victims Rights and Support Act 2013 contains the Charter of Victims Rights and the Victims Support Scheme, which can provide counselling and financial support. LEPRA deals with police powers, and the Bail Act with release before trial.

questions.stem: Which is an example of assistance available to victims of crime in NSW?
options: The right to sit on the jury in the trial of their offender
Counselling and financial support through the Victims Support Scheme
The power to decide whether the accused will be granted bail
The right to choose which charges the prosecution will bring
questions.explanation: The Victims Support Scheme offers counselling, financial assistance and recognition payments, and the Charter gives victims rights to information and respectful treatment. Bail and charging decisions are made by bail authorities and prosecutors, not victims.

questions.stem: In charge negotiation, an accused agrees to plead guilty to a less serious charge and the prosecution withdraws the more serious one. Which is the main benefit for the criminal justice system?
options: It guarantees that the offender will receive the longest sentence available
It allows the victim to decide the sentence that the offender will receive
It removes the need for the court to impose any sentence on the offender
It saves the time and cost of a trial and spares witnesses from giving evidence
questions.explanation: A negotiated plea avoids a lengthy trial, gives certainty and spares victims and witnesses, which is why it is common. The court still sentences the offender, and the offender is not guaranteed the maximum sentence.

questions.stem: A victim says a charge negotiation let the offender plead guilty to an offence that does not reflect what really happened. Which statement best evaluates this criticism?
options: Negotiations always produce the same sentence as a trial would have, so victims have no real reason to object
Negotiations are conducted in open court before a jury, so the community can always see how charges were chosen
Negotiations improve efficiency, but they can reduce transparency and leave victims feeling their harm was not recognised
Negotiations are never used in NSW for serious offences, so the criticism cannot apply to any indictable matter
questions.explanation: Charge negotiations happen privately between prosecution and defence, which saves resources but can make outcomes seem lenient and leave victims dissatisfied. NSW prosecutors are expected to consult victims, but the final decision rests with the prosecution.

questions.stem: Under the NSW early guilty plea scheme, an offender who pleads guilty to an indictable offence before committal to a higher court generally receives a sentence discount of:
options: 25 per cent
50 per cent
10 per cent
5 per cent
questions.explanation: The Crimes (Sentencing Procedure) Act 1999 sets a 25 per cent discount for a guilty plea before committal, 10 per cent for a plea after committal but well before trial, and 5 per cent otherwise. The scheme encourages early pleas that save court time and spare witnesses.

questions.stem: Bail is best described as:
options: an amount of money paid to a victim by an offender as part of the sentence imposed by the court
a court order that keeps an accused in custody until the end of the trial for public safety
the release of an accused person from custody while they wait for their case to be decided
the release of a convicted offender from prison before the end of the sentence under supervision
questions.explanation: Bail lets a person who has been charged but not convicted stay in the community, often on conditions, until the case is finished. Early release of a convicted offender under supervision is parole, and keeping an accused in custody is remand.

questions.stem: Under the Bail Act 2013 (NSW), a bail authority may refuse bail only if it is satisfied that:
options: there is an unacceptable risk that cannot be sufficiently reduced by bail conditions
the accused is more likely than not to be found guilty when the case finally goes to trial
the accused has any previous conviction recorded against them, of whatever kind
the police officer who made the arrest has asked the court to keep the accused in custody
questions.explanation: The Act requires the bail authority to assess bail concerns and refuse bail only for an unacceptable risk that conditions cannot adequately manage. Bail is not decided on the likely verdict, because the accused is presumed innocent.

questions.stem: Which is one of the bail concerns a NSW bail authority must assess?
options: That the accused will interfere with witnesses or evidence
That the accused will be unable to afford a private lawyer
That the accused has refused to answer police questions
That the accused intends to plead not guilty at trial
questions.explanation: The bail concerns are that the accused will fail to appear, commit a serious offence, endanger the safety of victims, individuals or the community, or interfere with witnesses or evidence. Staying silent or pleading not guilty are rights, not grounds for refusing bail.

questions.stem: For a show cause offence under the Bail Act 2013 (NSW), such as one punishable by life imprisonment, how is the bail decision different?
options: Bail must be granted automatically, because the seriousness of the charge makes it certain the accused will attend
The victim decides whether bail is granted, because show cause offences involve serious harm to a person
The bail authority must apply the criminal standard and be satisfied beyond reasonable doubt the accused is guilty
Bail must be refused unless the accused shows why detention is not justified, before the unacceptable risk test is applied
questions.explanation: For show cause offences the accused must first show cause why their detention is not justified; if they do, the bail authority then applies the unacceptable risk test. Critics argue this places a burden on a person who is still presumed innocent.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains the tension between bail laws and the presumption of innocence?
options: Refusing bail detains people who have not been convicted, but releasing everyone could put victims and the community at risk
Granting bail means the accused has been found not guilty, so the prosecution can no longer continue with the case
The presumption of innocence applies only after a jury verdict, so bail decisions have no effect on it at all
Bail can only be refused for summary offences, so serious offenders are always released whatever the risk
questions.explanation: An accused refused bail loses their liberty before any finding of guilt, yet the law must also protect victims, witnesses and the community. Bail laws try to balance these, and governments have often tightened them after high-profile offences committed on bail.

questions.stem: An accused person who is refused bail and held in custody until their case is decided is said to be:
options: on a bond
in diversion
on remand
on parole
questions.explanation: Remand is custody before a case is finished, for a person who is legally presumed innocent. Parole is supervised release after part of a sentence, and a bond is a sentencing order.

questions.stem: Which is a significant impact of remand on an accused person?
options: They must serve the full maximum sentence if they are later found guilty
They may lose their job or housing even though they have not been convicted
They are treated as convicted and their criminal record is updated straight away
They lose the right to plead not guilty when their case comes to court
questions.explanation: Time on remand can cost a person their employment, housing and family contact, and it can pressure them to plead guilty to get out sooner. If they are later sentenced to prison, time spent on remand is usually counted towards the sentence.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the impact of high remand numbers on society?
options: They increase prison costs and overcrowding, and some people held on remand are later acquitted or not jailed
They reduce prison costs, because people on remand are held in the community under supervision
They have no effect on prisons, because people on remand are kept in court cells rather than correctional centres
They guarantee lower crime rates, because every person on remand would otherwise have reoffended
questions.explanation: People on remand make up a large share of the NSW prison population, which adds to cost and overcrowding. Some are acquitted or receive a non-custodial sentence, which raises questions about whether their detention was justified.
